title: Virtual Triage A
subtitle: 8-month-old with respiratory distress
stem: It is 7:40 pm in the paediatric emergency room. A mother hurries in carrying her 8-month-old daughter. You are the triage nurse.
parent: "Sister, she has had a cold and cough for three days. Since this afternoon she is breathing very fast and she won't take the breast. She feels hot."

vitals.note: Irritable but consolable in mother's arms. Nasal flaring, subcostal and intercostal recessions, audible wheeze. Pink lips, warm hands. Room air.

decisions.title: Impression

options.text: Stable — a well infant with a cough; she can wait in the routine queue
options.outcome: You send her to the waiting queue. Twelve minutes later her mother rushes back: she has stopped crying and is breathing faster. SpO₂ 87 %, RR 66.
options.note: Two sides of the PAT are abnormal. Increased work of breathing with flaring and recessions is never "stable"; this child must not wait in the routine queue.

options.text: Unstable, non-life-threatening — breathing affected: respiratory distress
options.outcome: You take her straight past the queue to the triage bed, keep her upright on her mother’s lap and attach the monitor.
options.note: Unstable but not yet life-threatening: appearance is normal (consolable, good tone, interactive) while work of breathing is increased — respiratory distress, lower airway (wheeze). The infant is compensating, and compensation can be lost quickly at 8 months, so she needs treatment now and close watching.

options.text: Unstable, life-threatening — respiratory failure; start bag-mask ventilation
options.outcome: You call the resuscitation team and reach for the bag and mask. She is awake, consolable and fighting the mask; her chest is moving well. The team asks why she is being bagged.
options.note: In respiratory failure appearance is abnormal: lethargy, poor tone, not interacting, or a slowing or silent chest. She is irritable but consolable and interactive. Over-calling failure wastes the resuscitation bay; under-calling distress is the greater danger — reassess every few minutes.

options.text: Unstable — circulation affected: shock, because the heart rate is 168
options.outcome: You ask for an IV line and a fluid bolus. While the trolley is prepared nobody attends to her breathing; the recessions are deeper.
options.note: Tachycardia alone is not shock. Her circulation-to-skin side is normal: pink, warm, CRT 2 s. Fever, distress and crying all raise the heart rate. Shock needs abnormal circulation signs: pallor, mottling, cool extremities, delayed CRT.

options.text: Unstable — neurological: an irritable infant, check the brain first
options.outcome: You check her pupils and blood sugar and ask about fits. Meanwhile nobody attends to her breathing: the recessions are deeper and SpO₂ drifts to 87 %.
options.note: Her irritability comes from hypoxia and the work of breathing. She is consolable, with good tone and interaction, so appearance is normal — the problem is breathing.

must: respiratory distress or breathing affected (a nurse who names respiratory distress meets this; she need not write the words stable/unstable)

decisions.title: Intervention
decisions.prompt: What is your intervention? Choose all that apply.
decisions.key: Oxygen — non-rebreather mask (correct) or nasal cannula (acceptable) — and give the salbutamol nebulisation (correct); assessing ABCDE is acceptable alongside. Doing none of these is unsafe.

options.text: Start oxygen (NRM or nasal cannula) and give the salbutamol nebulisation
options.outcome: Oxygen on; she settles on her mother’s lap. The salbutamol nebulisation runs, driven with oxygen at 6–8 L/min. SpO₂ rises to 95 %, RR 56, HR 160.
options.note: Oxygen first, by whatever device she tolerates, to a target of 94–98 %; then treat the wheeze — prepare an oxygen-driven salbutamol nebulisation. Reassess within minutes.

options.text: Start oxygen only
options.outcome: SpO₂ creeps up to 94 %, but the wheeze and recessions are unchanged and she is still breathing at 62 a minute.
options.note: Oxygen treats the hypoxaemia, not the bronchospasm. With a wheeze, prepare the nebuliser at the same time.

options.text: Give the nebulisation without oxygen
options.outcome: The nebuliser hisses on a compressor. SpO₂ drifts down to 86 % and her heart rate climbs to 174.
options.note: A hypoxaemic child should be nebulised with oxygen (6–8 L/min), never with air; salbutamol can briefly worsen ventilation–perfusion mismatch.

options.text: Secure an IV line and send bloods first
options.outcome: Two attempts at a cannula. She screams and struggles: RR 70, HR 176, the recessions deepen.
options.note: An IV is not an A or B intervention, and the struggle will worsen her breathing. Nothing here needs IV access yet.

options.text: None of these — observe and recheck
options.outcome: Fifteen minutes later she is tiring: SpO₂ 86 %, HR 174, the cry is weaker.
options.note: SpO₂ 89 % with increased work of breathing is below the target of 94–98 %. Start oxygen now; observing does not treat hypoxaemia and the infant is tiring.

opts.v: Start oxygen — nasal cannula
Start oxygen — non-rebreather mask (NRM)
Assess ABCDE
Give salbutamol nebulisation
None of these

decisions.title: Reassessment
decisions.label: Your reassessment
decisions.prompt: Ten minutes later. Reassess her: what do you check, and what do you do next?

opts.v: Repeat the PAT and ABCDE: work of breathing, RR, HR, SpO₂
Stop the oxygen — SpO₂ is 95 % now
Listen to the chest: air entry and wheeze after the nebulisation
Score PEWS and chart it
Continue oxygen; repeat the nebulisation if the wheeze persists; recheck every 5–10 minutes
Check she can breastfeed and has passed urine
Move to the next patient and recheck at the next round

options.text: All the correct elements: Repeat the PAT and ABCDE: work of breathing, RR, HR, SpO₂; Listen to the chest: air entry and wheeze after the nebulisation; Continue oxygen; repeat the nebulisation if the wheeze persists; recheck every 5–10 minutes
options.outcome: RR 48, HR 150, SpO₂ 97 % on oxygen. The recessions ease and the wheeze is softer; she is starting to look around. The treatment is working — and she still needs oxygen.
options.note: Reassess after every intervention and every 5–10 minutes while she is unstable: PAT, ABCDE and the chest. Better numbers on oxygen do not mean she is ready to come off it.

options.text: Some correct elements, nothing unsafe (partial)
options.outcome: You record some numbers but not the full picture. Ten minutes later her mother calls you: RR 60, SpO₂ 93 %, the recessions are back. A full PAT, ABCDE and chest check would have caught it earlier.

options.text: Stop the oxygen — SpO₂ is 95 % now
options.outcome: Off oxygen she drifts to SpO₂ 88 % within minutes; RR 64, HR 172. The monitor alarms.

options.text: Move to the next patient and recheck at the next round
options.outcome: Nobody reassesses her. Thirty minutes later she is tiring: SpO₂ 90 %, RR 66, HR 172, the recessions deeper.

decisions.title: Communication with the parents
decisions.label: Your communication with the mother
decisions.prompt: Her mother is crying: “Sister, what is happening to her? Why the mask? Will she be all right?”

opts.v: Introduce yourself and explain in simple words, in her language: her chest is tight, the oxygen and the nebuliser help her breathe
“Don’t worry, it is nothing serious”
Keep the baby on her lap and let her help hold the mask
Ask her to wait outside so the team can work
Tell her what happens next — admission and monitoring — and which signs to call you for
Ask what she has understood and whether she has questions

options.text: All the correct elements: Introduce yourself and explain in simple words, in her language: her chest is tight, the oxygen and the nebuliser help her breathe; Keep the baby on her lap and let her help hold the mask; Tell her what happens next — admission and monitoring — and which signs to call you for
options.outcome: The mother calms and holds the mask close to her daughter’s face; the baby settles on her lap. She repeats back: “If she breathes faster or stops feeding, I call you.”
options.note: Parents are part of the team: honest, simple words in their language, a job at the bedside, and clear signs to call you.

options.text: Some correct elements, nothing unsafe (partial)
options.outcome: She nods but looks lost. A few minutes later she lifts the mask off to feed the baby and the SpO₂ dips to 92 %.

options.text: “Don’t worry, it is nothing serious”
options.outcome: She relaxes — and when the doctor later talks of admission she is angry and frightened: “But sister said it was nothing.” Her trust in the team is lost.

options.text: Ask her to wait outside so the team can work
options.outcome: Away from her mother the baby screams and fights the mask: RR 60, HR 168, SpO₂ 92 %.

decisions.title: Team communication
decisions.label: Your communication with the doctor
decisions.prompt: The registrar answers your call. What do you say and do?

opts.v: ISBAR with numbers: who you are, the child, situation, background, assessment (SpO₂ 89 → 97 %, RR 64 → 48), recommendation
“Doctor, the baby is not looking good, please come”
Ask for a clear action and a time: “Please review her within 15 minutes”
Read back every order you are given (closed loop)
Chart the times of the oxygen and the nebulisation
Write it in the notes and tell the doctor at the next round

options.text: All the correct elements: ISBAR with numbers: who you are, the child, situation, background, assessment (SpO₂ 89 → 97 %, RR 64 → 48), recommendation; Ask for a clear action and a time: “Please review her within 15 minutes”; Read back every order you are given (closed loop)
options.outcome: “Clear, sister — I am coming. Continue the oxygen and repeat the nebulisation if the wheeze returns.” You read the order back; she is reviewed within 10 minutes.
options.note: Speak with a number, not an adjective: ISBAR, a clear request with a time, and closed-loop read-back of every order.

options.text: Some correct elements, nothing unsafe (partial)
options.outcome: The registrar has to ask three questions to get the numbers and what you want; the review is delayed by 15 minutes.

options.text: “Doctor, the baby is not looking good, please come”
options.outcome: “How bad is she? I am busy in the ward.” Without numbers the call goes into the queue; she is seen 40 minutes later.

options.text: Write it in the notes and tell the doctor at the next round
options.outcome: No one senior knows about her. An hour later she is tiring on the trolley: SpO₂ 91 %, RR 64, HR 170.

decisions.title: Transfer
decisions.label: Your transfer plan
decisions.prompt: The registrar asks you to move her. Where does she go, and how?

opts.v: Admit to the paediatric HDU / a monitored ward bed
Discharge home on salbutamol syrup; review in OPD tomorrow
Move her on oxygen with a pulse oximeter, a nurse escort and her mother with her
Admit to the PICU
Call ahead: the receiving bed has oxygen, suction and a monitor ready
Let the mother carry her to the ward; oxygen can start there

options.text: All the correct elements: Admit to the paediatric HDU / a monitored ward bed; Move her on oxygen with a pulse oximeter, a nurse escort and her mother with her; Call ahead: the receiving bed has oxygen, suction and a monitor ready
options.outcome: She reaches the HDU on oxygen, saturating 97 %, her mother beside her. The bed is ready and the HDU nurse takes your ISBAR handover.
options.note: Right place, right way: a monitored bed matched to her needs, moved on oxygen with monitoring and an escort, the receiving team ready before she arrives.

options.text: Some correct elements, nothing unsafe (partial)
options.outcome: She gets there, but not everything was in place: on arrival the team sets up oxygen and the monitor while she goes unwatched for several minutes.

options.text: Discharge home on salbutamol syrup; review in OPD tomorrow
options.outcome: Twelve hours later she is brought back by ambulance, grey and exhausted: SpO₂ 84 %, RR 70, HR 180.

options.text: Let the mother carry her to the ward; oxygen can start there
options.outcome: Halfway down the corridor without oxygen she turns dusky: SpO₂ 86 %, HR 174.

debrief: What was your impression, and which findings made her unstable but not yet life-threatening?
Why oxygen first, and why prepare the nebuliser at the same time?
What did you look at on reassessment, and what would have made you upgrade her to Level 1?
takeHome: Impression first: stable or unstable, life-threatening or not, and which system — here, unstable non-life-threatening respiratory distress.
Intervention: oxygen (non-rebreather mask, or nasal cannula) and an oxygen-driven salbutamol nebulisation for the wheeze.
Reassess after every intervention and every 5 minutes while unstable; give the treatment you prepared and escalate with ISBAR.
references: AHA PALS Provider Manual 2020: Pediatric Assessment Triangle, respiratory distress and failure, oxygen therapy.
IAP ICC PCCN Module 01: PAT, ABCDE, triage levels, DIRECT approach.

ending.smooth: The registrar confirms bronchiolitis and admits her to the HDU on nasal prongs. By the next morning she is feeding at the breast and the recessions are settling.
ending.detour: She reaches the doctor and the HDU, but the detours meant a longer spell of hypoxaemia and a tiring infant; she needed high-flow oxygen on admission.
